parents how to have zeal for the Law and for God, and he knew exactly where he needed 
to be.  
(Source: James Burton Coffman Commentaries) This is the first recorded utterance of Jesus; and, in it, he 
laid claim to a relationship to Almighty God, in a sense that distinguished his relationship from one that is 
open to other men; and throughout his ministry, this claim of Jesus was often repeated. 
50 But they did not understand the statement which he had made to them. 51 And he went 
down with them and came to Nazareth, and he continued in subjection to them; and his 
mother treasured all these things in her heart. 52 And Jesus kept increasing in wisdom and 
stature, and in favor with God and men.  
God’s influence was working through his parents, enabling them to teach him an 
appreciation of the ways of God that would deepen as he grew up. We know many 
mothers who are thrilled when their children have any propensity towards God, and we 
can hear Mary’s quiet joy in Jesus. 

His mother treasured all these things in her heart―she saw him growing into the man who 
would change the world. We can imagine she is sitting there in awe of this boy as he is 
becoming the man who would be the Messiah after his baptism. 
God allowed this potential tragedy of Jesus’ separation from his parents as a message to 
them and to onlookers. Even as a boy, Jesus was focused on his heavenly Father.  
Real Zeal Roots: True zeal, because it is a constant and 
disciplined lifestyle, can dramatically affect others.  
Mary and Joseph’s unwavering and faithful example taught Jesus 
what unwavering faith and zeal looked like. Their example gave 
him permission to live his zeal for his heavenly Father! 
Let’s not underestimate the power of passing on zeal and faith to our children. 
At first glance, we can see that zeal for God is a reverential application of our heart and 
mind to outwardly stand for godliness.  
In the New Testament, “being on fire” for Christ began before Jesus  
was even born. How did Jesus focus us on that zeal in his ministry?  
There is never a time we will be disappointed by looking at Jesus’ own life as an example of 
how to do things. His faithful upbringing, his perfect mind and God’s spirit always 
combined as teaching tools with no equal. We will begin by focusing on the event in his 
life where his disciples recalled and applied the power of David’s zeal for God’s house, and 
then applied it to Jesus. 
John 2:13–17: 13 The Passover of the Jews was near, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. 14 And he 
found in the temple <2411> those who were selling oxen and sheep and doves, and the money 
changers seated at their tables. 15 And he made a scourge of cords, and drove them all out of 
the temple, with the sheep and the oxen; and he poured out the coins of the money changers 
and overturned their tables; 16 and to those who were selling the doves he said, Take these 
things away; stop making my Father’s house a place of business. 17 His disciples remembered 
that it was written (in Psalm 69:9), ZEAL <2205> FOR YOUR HOUSE WILL CONSUME ME.  
His disciples quoted our theme scripture! We now know this refers back to King David’s 
zeal to build a dwelling place for God. Let’s tie this together. Jesus is in the Temple—what 
does temple mean here? 
This Greek word for temple means “a sacred place.” It’s used in the New Testament to 
describe the entire Temple complex in Jerusalem with all its buildings, courts, etc. It’s also 
used to describe the pagan Temple of Artemis. Just like in the Old Testament, the Greek 
word for zeal here means “ardor or jealousy.” We’re carrying over what King David 
experienced into the New Testament. 

Zeal: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2205 zelos; properly, heat, i.e. (figuratively) "zeal" 
(in a favorable sense, ardor; in an unfavorable one, jealousy, as of a husband  
[figuratively, of God], or an enemy, malice) 
In its highest sense, zeal transforms our emotion into a positive action.  
Was Jesus’ zeal here a meltdown, temper tantrum type of zeal? Was he out of control? 
Jesus was never out of control. Notice how he treated the doves―only the poor could 
afford them for their sacrifices, so Jesus did not release them as they would have 
flown away. The other animals could easily have been brought back. He was purposeful in 
his actions.  He was controlled. He had an objective: to cleanse his Father’s house from 
being a place of business.  
This money changing (usury) did not belong in God’s house. He did what was necessary to 
disrupt what did not belong. He wasn’t so angry that his face turned red and he was out‐
of‐control angry. He was forceful, wielding a small whip, as he went about the releasing of 
the animals and sweeping off the tables just as far as was necessary to show his point. The 
treatment of the doves shows us his control and how he cared for the poor.  

Those in charge were not happy with this and they demanded to know what right Jesus 
had to act in this way.  
Interestingly, yet not surprisingly, Jesus did not answer them. Instead, he spoke 
what sounded like a riddle, but it was in fact a deeply prophetic statement: 
John 2:18–22: 18 The Jews then said to him, What sign do you show us as your authority for 
doing these things? 19 Jesus answered them, destroy this temple <3485>, and in three days I 
will raise it up.  
They must have thought, What kind of ridiculous answer is this? 
20 The Jews then said, It took forty‐six years to build this temple <3485>, and will you raise it 
up in three days? 21 But he was speaking of the temple <3485> of his body. 22 So when he was 
raised  from  the  dead,  his  disciples  remembered  that  he  said  this;  and  they  believed  the 
scripture and the word which Jesus had spoken. 
So, this wasn’t about the physical building. This was an allusion to his being 
resurrected―a much bigger meaning! 

The Greek word for temple here isn’t the same as the reference to the entire Temple 
complex. This word is used only to indicate the two sacred rooms called the Holy and the 
Most Holy. This subtle but important point is missed when translating into English. 
Temple: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3485 naos;  
(to dwell); a fane, shrine, temple 
 The King James Version translates this as temple 45 times, a shrine 1 time 
Thayer’s Greek‐English Lexicon: 1) used of the temple at Jerusalem,  
but only of the sacred edifice (or sanctuary) itself, consisting of the Holy place  
and the Holy of Holies 2) any heathen temple or shrine 3) metaphorically the spiritual 
temple consisting of the saints of all ages joined together by and in Christ 
“Temple” here refers to these two sacred rooms. How could these rooms be his physical 
body? What “temple” was Jesus REALLY speaking about? 
While there was a reference in his words to his resurrection, his deep prophetic 
message was about his followers, who would soon be known as the “body of Christ.” 
1 Corinthians 12:27: Now you are Christ's body, and individually members of it. 
These “body members” are regularly referred to as God’s “temple,” the same Greek word 
for temple as the two sacred rooms. So, when Jesus speaks about raising up his body, we 
can see the prophetic meaning as referring to his true disciples. The zeal of thine house—
the zeal of protecting the sanctity of the true church had consumed him.  
1 Corinthians 3:16: Do you not know that you are a temple <3485> of God and that the spirit 
of God dwells in you?  
The word for temple here is again that same Greek word for the two sacred rooms of the 
Holy and Most Holy. In other words, YOU are where God dwells, just like in the 
Tabernacle and Temple back in ancient days.  
There is a powerful connection between Jesus’ statement about raising up the “temple” 
and the spirit of God dwelling in the most faithful followers of Jesus. He would “raise up” 
his church throughout the two centuries of the age of the gospel message going forth. 
TRUE FOLLOWERS OF CHRIST ARE A SANCTUARY IN WHICH GOD’S SPIRIT 
DWELLS.  
The connection between the words of Jesus to the Pharisees directly correlates to the body 
of Christ―not only his physical body, but his spiritual body we just read as described in  
1 Corinthians 12:27 that includes all of his faithful followers. There is a double meaning. 
God’s presence still exists in this world centuries after the Temple in Jerusalem was 
destroyed in 70 AD. Where is God’s spirit―His inﬂuence―maintained now? Within the 
true brotherhood; in the “new creatures” in Christ as described in 2 Corinthians 5:17. 

That’s profound. No wonder the Pharisees were confounded by Jesus! This was far beyond 
them! He was teaching them something so much bigger.  
Let’s go back to our question, “Is my life on fire for Christ?” Having God’s spirit dwelling 
within us is where the fire comes from! It is not from our emotions or our thinking. It is 
from God’s spirit igniting that flame to serve Him. This is exactly what happened to Jesus 
when he was baptized―God’s spirit descended upon him and dwelt within him.  
As Jesus cleansed the temple of moral unrighteousness, so we should be cleansed 
as well: 
1 Corinthians 6:17–20: 17 But the one who joins himself to the Lord is one spirit with Him. 
 18 Flee immorality. Every other sin that a man commits is outside the body, but the immoral 
man sins against his own body. 19 Or do you not know that your body is a temple <3485> 
(referring only to the sacred structures) of the holy spirit (which) is in you, whom you have 
from God, and that you are not your own? 20 For you have been bought with a price: therefore 
glorify God in your body.  
It's a common expression to say, “Your body is a temple” when people are exercising or 
eating healthy foods. We don’t think they understand what this phrase means. The phrase 
is actually—Your body is a temple of the holy spirit which is in you. If we are faithful 
Christians, we are housing the presence of God and should have the same zeal King David 
used in his preparations. We are a sacred space. This opens up a whole new way of 
thinking about not only what we put into our bodies or the reckless behaviors that could 
damage it, but our own attitude if we only see imperfections in our body image or are 
discouraged with our declining health.  
Understand the position we’ve been called to! This is a highly reverential place to be and 
requires great zeal to manage and maintain. When we talk about having “zeal for Christ,” 
this is where it comes from. It goes beyond just a feeling to something powerfully deep 
and life‐changing. 
Collectively with Jesus, we are the sanctuary where God dwells: 
Ephesians 2:20–22: 20 having been built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, 
Christ  Jesus  himself  being  the  corner  stone,  21  in  whom  the  whole  building,  being  fitted 
together, is growing into a holy temple <3485> in the Lord, 22 in whom you also are being built 
together into a dwelling of God in the spirit. 
Let's fast forward to today. Jesus clearing the Temple gave us the example to protect the 
sanctity of the body members, which is the “spiritual temple.” Whenever Churchianity 
makes Christianity into a business full of corruption and immorality, we have an 
obligation to remove ourselves from those false systems. This is why it says in Revelation 
18:4: Come out of her my people. There’s a lot more to the application of Jesus’ statement of 
raising up the body in three days, but that’s for a future episode. 

In whom the whole building, being fitted together, is growing into a holy temple in the 
Lord―refers to the faithful followers of Jesus with Jesus himself as the cornerstone. He’s 
the model for this whole building made up of true Christians gathered for the last 2,000 
years! 
This is such a motivational force—not just to feel good, but to be different―to be 
transformed. 

When Jesus spoke of his “body,” we see the spiritual meaning in Jesus’ words. The further 
we go, the more powerfully the whole concept of zeal for God is revealed. This is 
becoming an intense journey! 
From just this one account we can see the depth of Jesus’ zeal.  
How do we translate that into our own Christian lives?  
We obviously cannot do the things Jesus did and speak in prophetic ways as he spoke. 
What we CAN do is identify the thoughts, words and actions that exemplify a zeal for God 
through Jesus that can permeate our very lives every day. To begin this process, we need 
to realize that zeal can be very positive and transformational OR very negative and 
debilitating. 
As we discussed, Jesus got angry, but he was never out of control. He was purposeful. 
My goal for this year has been to live each day with a spiritual focus. I'm getting 
the sense that “zeal” and “purposeful” fit together as a driving force to honor God. 
Jesus was purposeful and intentional.  
The Apostle Paul was also purposeful—this one thing I do―Philippians 3:13 (KJV). We 
see that powerful intention and purposeful thoughts precede purposeful action. This is 
what having our lives on fire for Christ is.  
Let’s look at some of the issues that come with zeal. In Revelation, the message to the 
church at Laodicea reveals chronic misplaced zeal that leads to confused priorities and an 
ungodly outcome. 

This admonition shows something must change: 
Revelation 3:14–19: 14 To the angel of the church in Laodicea write… 15 I know your deeds, 
that you are neither cold nor hot; I wish that you were cold or hot. 16 So because you are 
lukewarm, and neither hot nor cold, I will spit you out of my mouth. 17 Because you say, I am 
rich, and have become wealthy, and have need of nothing, and you do not know that you are 
wretched and miserable and poor and blind and naked, 18 I advise you to buy from me gold 
refined by fire so that you may become rich, and white garments so that you may clothe 
yourself, and that the shame of your nakedness will not be revealed; and eye salve to anoint 
your eyes so that you may see. 19 Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline; therefore be 
zealous <2206> and repent.  
Zeal: Thayer’s Greek‐English Lexicon 1) to burn with zeal  
1a) to be heated or to boil with envy, hatred, anger 
We see again that the word can go either in a positive, strong direction or in a negative, 
debilitating direction. The obvious meaning here is a message to be zealous―be driven 
and repent―because what you have seen yourself to be is not what you really are.  
The prophetic problem in the church of Laodicea is they 
were lukewarm, being sort of middle of the road. They were 
not too committed. They were happy being non‐committal. 
They were feeling good about themselves because things 
were going well. They lived comfortably in a material sense.  
Then they got the message that NO, it was not going well! 
They were poor and blind and naked. They were not able to see this. This was the message. 
Their calling was MUCH more than what they felt. As a result, they were severely 
admonished towards change. 
Laodicea was a real city which is still in present‐day Turkey. A more recent interpretation 
suggested that this hot/cold metaphor was about the city’s water supply. 
(Source: Wikipedia) “…that was lukewarm, in contrast to the hot springs at nearly 
Hierapolis and the cold, pure waters of Colossae. The archaeology shows that Laodicea 
had an aqueduct that probably carried water from hot mineral springs some five miles 
south, which would have become tepid before entering the city. The imagery of the 
Laodicean aqueduct suggests not that "hot" is good and "cold" is bad, but that both hot 
and cold water are useful, whereas lukewarm water is emetic (an agent used to induce 
vomiting).”  
That’s such a great description of not being in a good place and the need to change. 

ZEAL THAT BREAKS US DOWN—MISDIRECTED ZEAL:  
Israel’s zeal under the Law when their Messiah came: 
Romans 9:31–32: 31 but Israel, pursuing a law of righteousness, did not arrive at that law. 32 
Why? Because they did not pursue it by faith, but as though it were by works. They stumbled 
over the stumbling stone. 
Israel was so “works‐oriented” that when their Messiah came, they stumbled over him 
instead of embracing him.  
They should have seen Jesus for what he was, but instead he got in the way of their 
predetermined agenda and things were misdirected as a result: 
Romans 10:1–4: 1 Brethren, my heart's desire and my prayer to God for them is for their 
salvation.  2  For  I  testify  about  them  that  they  have  a  zeal  <2205>  for  God,  but  not  in 
accordance with knowledge. 3 For not knowing about God's righteousness and seeking to 
establish their own, they did not subject themselves to the righteousness of God. 4 For Christ 
is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.  
They had a zeal for God, but that zeal drove them down the wrong road. They did not have 
the right knowledge. Their zeal was misdirected because they were looking for the 
Messiah to come as a mighty warrior to free them from the rule of the Romans. But this 
was not Jesus’ mission. Their preconceived ideas gave their zeal a misdirection. How do we 
handle this problem in our own lives?  
Breaking down zeal that breaks us down: Look in the mirror. Be sure that 
our zeal is based upon that which is spiritually true rather than that which is 
comfortable or traditional. 
Laodicea became comfortable and traditional and they were chastised for being poor, blind 
and naked. How can we counteract that? 
ZEAL THAT BUILDS—GODLY ZEAL:  
2 Corinthians 11:2–3: 2 For I am jealous <2206> for you with a godly jealousy <2205>; for I 
betrothed you to one husband, so that to Christ I might present you as a pure virgin. 3 But I 
am afraid that, as the serpent deceived Eve by his craftiness, your minds will be led astray from 
the simplicity and purity of devotion to Christ. 
This is a godly jealousy, godly zeal, so it’s not negative. Godly zeal is ultimately about well‐
being, not destroying. We can see the difference between misdirected zeal and godly zeal.  

The Apostle Paul is saying, I am jealous over you , and I am going to take serious action to 
make sure you are protected because you are betrothed to Christ. This is an action, not a 
feeling or thought. You are far too important, and therefore I will act on it. 
ZEAL THAT BREAKS US DOWN—ZEAL AS A TOOL OF DISCONTENT: 
James 3:13–16: 13 Who among you is wise and understanding? Let him show by his good 
behavior his deeds in the gentleness of wisdom. 14 But if you have bitter jealousy <2205> and 
selfish ambition in your heart, do not be arrogant and so lie against the truth. 15 This wisdom 
is not that which comes down from above, but is earthly, natural, demonic. 16 For where 
jealousy <2205> and selfish ambition exist, there is disorder and every evil thing.  
This describes the wrong kind of jealousy/zeal. It is bitter, selfish and untruthful. This 
kind of jealousy feeds discontent which leaves no room for gratitude. It’s a quick road to 
nowhere good. 
We see the difference—we can have jealousy for good or jealousy for evil. We need to 
make sure our Christian zeal is always driven by righteousness for the upbuilding of those 
around us. 
Breaking down zeal that breaks us down: Look in the mirror. Recognize 
what motivated our INWARD feelings in the past and decisively act to replace 
those self‐serving feelings with God‐honoring contributions to others. 
We are not trying to replace emotion with a bigger emotion; we’re trying to take our 
emotion and expand it into action. 
Godly zeal is not about how we feel, it is about what we do!  
ZEAL THAT BUILDS:  
Romans 15:1–3: 1 Now we who are strong ought to bear the weaknesses of those without 
strength and not just please ourselves. 2 Each of us is to please his neighbor for his good, to 
his  edification.  3  For  even  Christ  did  not  please  himself;  but  as  it  is  written,  THE 
REPROACHES OF THOSE WHO REPROACHED YOU FELL ON ME. 
One theme here is not pleasing ourselves; rather, pleasing our neighbor and taking care of 
others. The theme of the previous scriptures was jealousy and selfish ambition.  
We can see the difference—SELFISHNESS versus SELFLESSNESS. We should be thinking 
of others, as this is what “being on fire for Christ” is about. 
ZEAL THAT BREAKS US DOWN—ZEAL USED FOR DARK PURPOSES EVEN WITH 
GOOD INTENTIONS:  
We have a clear example of this with the Apostle Paul describing his former life as Saul. 
He let the experience of his past sins, in a good way, become a teaching tool for others. 
Paul describes his past credentials: 
Philippians 3:4–6: 4 although I myself might have confidence even in the flesh. If anyone else 
has a mind to put confidence in the flesh, I far more: 5 circumcised the eighth day, of the nation 

of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews; as to the Law, a Pharisee; 6 as to zeal 
<2205>,  a  persecutor  of  the  church;  as  to  the  righteousness  which  is  in  the  Law,  found 
blameless. 
As Saul, he very passionately persecuted Christians, trying to force them to blaspheme, 
and even going so far as to have them killed.  
Saul’s intention was to serve God, but he was doing it completely the wrong way. He was 
feeding and supporting darkness. He was stepping outside the confines of the Law 
thinking he was doing the right thing, but he wasn’t. He was using good intentions in the 
wrong way. 
Zeal takes us somewhere. Zeal for darkness takes us down a dark road. Zeal for light and 
righteousness takes us down a bright road. 
Breaking down zeal that breaks us down: Look in the mirror. Recognize 
what motivated our OUTWARD sinful actions in the past (just like Paul did!) 
and decisively act to replace the darkness of twisted earthly ambition with the 
light of the true Gospel. Now, zealously act accordingly. 
ZEAL THAT BUILDS:  
In contrast, let’s look at a straightforward scripture from the Apostle Paul himself, 
who just previously referred to his zeal in a negative sense: 
Philippians 1:21: For to me, to live is Christ and to die is gain.  
To die is gain—we don’t fear death, as our life is consumed by following in the footsteps of 
Jesus. 
Spiritually productive zeal is hard to come by, and applying it includes consciously 
identifying where our motivations have come from. 
How can we learn to detect the differences between our  
positive emotions and spiritually-productive zeal?  
Confusion between positive emotional stimulation and godly zeal is an easy trap to fall 
into. When we get emotionally charged about a biblical teaching or from a fellowship 
experience, we get this sense that we are seeing clearly and things will be different. While 
these things may be good attention getters, they are not true zeal. However, they CAN 

identify the motivations that drive the true zeal of a dedicated Christian life. We need to 
be able to distinguish between emotion and zeal. 
We’re seeing that zeal is more than just an emotion; godly zeal means transformation!  
It means taking action! What are we going to DO with our zeal? If we are not taking 
action in some way, then our zeal is not engaged and will fizzle out over time.   
Let’s look at a comparison between emotions and zeal.  
Emotion: I am so excited to be in church today. Isn’t it wonderful? 
Yes! It's something to be excited about, and we don't want to ever lose that 
feeling. 
Zeal: My desire to be with and uplift the brotherhood provokes me to be in church 
 each and every time I am capable, not just for today. 
Hebrews 10:23–25: 23 Let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering, for He 
who promised is faithful; 24 and let us consider how to stimulate one another to love and good 
deeds, 25 not forsaking our own assembling together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging 
one another; and all the more as you see the day drawing near. 
It is not enough to be excited to be in church; what am I doing with that excitement? Who 
am I touching? How am I blessing those around me? I may hear beautiful things, but what 
am I giving back? It is a give‐and‐take. Zeal is letting whatever is within us come out. It is 
action, not just a good feeling.  
Hebrews 10:24 was our original theme scripture for the very first Christian 
Questions broadcast  almost 26 years ago to the day when we were on a local 
Connecticut radio station. We continue today to have this same goal of stimulating 
one another to love and good deeds! 
In terms of zeal, the most fertile learning experience of my entire Christian life in 
relation to zeal is Christian Questions. When we started, it was exciting. There was 
a lot of emotion. It was so great to have this opportunity. Then one day, it settled 
in—wait a minute, we have to do this every single week! 
I hadn’t thought about that. Every single week after 
week, month after month, year after year. This is where 
zeal was learned and continues to be learned. I learned 
more about zeal in this work than in any other single 
aspect of my own Christian walk. 
It has been one of the greatest blessings as a result, 
because we realize we are far more capable than we 
think, IF we rely on God’s grace, God’s spirit, God’s 
providence and strength. That is the way zeal can work 
in our lives. 

Emotion: I love to hear God’s word preached as it makes me feel 
energized! 
And it should! We should embrace that feeling of energy. 
Zeal: My focus is continually growing and maturing as I strive to implement what  
I hear. 
There’s that consistency we talked about before. It takes a long time to change our habits. 
Maturity doesn’t come quickly! 
James 1:21–24: 21 Therefore, putting aside all filthiness and all that remains of wickedness, in 
humility receive the word implanted, which is able to save your souls. 22 But prove yourselves 
doers of the word, and not merely hearers who delude themselves. 23 For if anyone is a hearer 
of the word and not a doer, he is like a man who looks at his natural face in a mirror; 24 for 
once he has looked at himself and gone away, he has immediately forgotten what kind of 
person he was. 
It's good to feel energized, but we have to go further―how can I expand that emotion to 
create change for me to be a stronger Christian?  
Be a doer of the word. Hear it, appreciate it, absorb it and act on it! This is where true 
Christian zeal can begin to grow and mature. It is wonderful to feel energized. It’s even 
better to have that energy provoke positive spiritual action. 
Emotion: Every day I wake up and thank God that He accepts me as  
I am! After all, Christianity is “come as you are.” We are called from all 
walks of life.  
What a wonderful thing to be grateful for. Lord, thank you for taking me as I am. It is 
incredibly important to have such gratitude. 
Zeal: Knowing God through Jesus has accepted me with my shortcomings provokes 
me to daily walk in self‐denial.  
Christianity might be “come as you are,” but it’s not “stay as you are.” It’s “come up 
higher:” 
Romans 12:1–2: 1 Therefore I urge you, brethren, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies 
a living and holy sacrifice, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service of worship. 2 And 
do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that 
you may prove what the will of God is, that which is good and acceptable and perfect.  
Christian zeal has everything to do with Christian transformation. Do not be conformed…, 
but be transformed by the renewing of your mind. How are our minds renewed? By God’s 
spirit. Remember that verse about God’s spirit and you being the “temple” of God’s spirit? 

This is who we are and where our responsibility and focus are. God is present through His 
power and influence—His spirit―in us every single day. 
Wherever we go, whatever we say, whatever we do, we are carrying God’s spirit with us. 
We cannot take this lightly! It is wonderful to say, Lord, thank You for accepting me as I 
am, but it is SO much more important to say, Lord transform me through Your spirit! Help 
me to do the work so that I can become a mature servant of Yours.  
Emotion: I am so privileged to be able to read the Bible! So many 
people today and in generations past never had this opportunity.  
This IS a great privilege!  
Zeal is: The depth and power of the Bible provokes me to regularly 
 study it to the best of my ability. 
2 Timothy 2:15–16: 15 Be diligent to present yourself approved to God as a workman who does 
not need to be ashamed, accurately handling the word of truth. 16 But avoid worldly and empty 
chatter, for it will lead to further ungodliness,  
In order to be accurately handling the word of truth (the Bible), we have to put in the time 
to study.  
It is wonderful to read the Bible but even more blessed to STUDY and learn. Using tools 
like these CQ Rewind Show Notes are a help to increase our zeal. Effective Bible study 
requires our focus and energy. Chrisitan zeal is an expending of energy toward godly 
purposes. 

Emotion: God called me out of the darkness of the world!  
I am blessed! 
If we have been called out of darkness, we certainly are blessed! 
Zeal: I am continuously aware that others might need to be touched with the 
 gospel of the kingdom, and I am eager to be a witness in words and actions. 

Romans 10:14–15: 14 How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? How 
will they believe in him whom they have not heard? And how will they hear without a preacher? 
15 How will they preach unless they are sent? Just as it is written, HOW BEAUTIFUL ARE THE 
FEET OF THOSE WHO BRING GOOD NEWS OF GOOD THINGS! 
It’s great to feel good about being called out of darkness, but it’s better to then be a 
witness to others and pass it on. Sometimes words don’t work, but actions do. Integrity 
does. These are all a part of Christian zeal every day of our lives.  

Are we living daily to be a witness to those around us? Or are we just going along like the 
Laodicean Christians, ending up poor, blind, wretched and naked?  
Looking prophetically at the experience of Jesus on the cross: 
Isaiah 50:6–7: 6 I gave my back to those who strike me, and my cheeks to those who pluck 
out the beard; I did not cover my face from humiliation and spitting. 7 For the Lord GOD helps

Jesus’ Resurrection – What Changed?
John 21:12: (NASB) Jesus said to them, Come and have breakfast.
None of the disciples ventured to question him, Who are you?
knowing that it was the Lord.
After the greatest act of love ever committed, Jesus lay dead
in a donated tomb. His loyal companions and followers were
stunned, sickened by what they had witnessed. But beyond
the gory details of this death, they were hit with the
uncomfortable thought that perhaps all they had known the
past three and a half years was a lie, fake, delusional. This
man, Jesus, they had trusted and loved was dead. He died
like everyone else.
There was no last-minute fire from
heaven to kill the Roman soldiers or the angry mob of his own
brethren demanding his death. There was no angelic rescue
team to pull him off that dreaded piece of wood.
He was
dead. For real. No one was coming to save them from the
Roman rule.
They would not be sitting on anyone’s right
hand in the new government. They had seemingly been duped. Now what? Well,
three days later, it was imperative that the risen Jesus convince them beyond a
shadow of doubt that all he had promised was REAL and was happening.
His
followers needed to be 100% convinced and energized to tell the Good News at
any cost to all who would listen. The man Jesus was gone forever, but the spirit
Jesus would have life within himself and power to restore all of mankind back to
his Father. They needed to urgently tell that story to you and me. How did the
disciples go from feeling ultimate betrayal and grief to absolute certainty and
joy?
To set our context, we will begin with a partial quote from the book, Moments
with the Savior.
An Intense Moment on the Emmaus Road, Moments with the Savior, Ken Gire
(Only an excerpt from the reading is shown here. Please listen to the audio of our
program or refer to the book.)
•
It is called Good Friday. But for these two followers of
Jesus nothing about it is good. Everything good this day
has died. And it seems to them it will be Friday for the
rest of their lives. For the rest of Jerusalem, though,
it’s Sunday. The Passover Sabbath is over, and life has
returned to normal. But for these two men the sounds
of life returning to normal seems a sacrilege. For them
nothing could ever be normal again. No Passover could
come without memories of him who was led as a lamb to
the slaughter.
No sacrifice could be made without
remembering the way he was sheared and cut up and
stretched out on that God-forsaken cross.
Since these
two were friends of the man on that cross, a lot of
strangers wanted to ask them questions, find out exactly what happened, and
exactly what the disciples were going to do now.
But the two were so
disoriented from grief they didn’t know anything vaguely, let alone exactly.

And what they did know, they didn’t want to talk about.
Especially with
strangers. And since the city was a spilling silo of strangers, they wanted out.
They decide the country would be a good place to go, where there is space to
think, to sort things out.
And they have plenty to sort.
They have left
everything behind to follow Jesus. They have staked their future on his words
– their hopes, their dreams, everything. Now he is gone. And somehow, they
will have to get along without him.
Our podcast is all about tragedy, doubt and clarity. When we go through the
all too familiar life experiences of tragedy and doubt what we find is that we
are always seeking clarity to balance them, to help us cope with and overcome
them. At the time of Jesus’ crucifixion and death his followers were
overwhelmed in tragedy and doubt, the risen Jesus sought to prove to them
that the seemingly incomprehensible facts of his resurrection and change were
not only factual, but the most world-changing factual events that would ever
occur. Giving his followers clarity in such immense and unique circumstances
would not be easy. But Jesus is good at “not easy” and this is the story of how
he would help his followers to see, absorb and stand for his cause as their risen
Messiah.
The revealing of Jesus’ resurrection came in steps – small steps - as the
magnitude of change and significance that needed to be absorbed by his
followers was overwhelming.
We begin with the first hint that Jesus was alive:
Matthew 28:1-7: (NASB) 1Now after the Sabbath, as it began to dawn toward the first day
of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary (and Salome) came to look at the grave.
2And behold, a severe earthquake had occurred, for an angel of the Lord descended from
heaven and came and rolled away the stone and sat upon it. 3And his appearance was like
lightning, and his clothing as white as snow. 4The guards shook for fear of him and became like
dead men. 5The angel said to the women, Do not be afraid; for I know that you are looking for
Jesus who has been crucified. 6He is not here, for he has risen, just as he said. Come, see the
place where he was lying. 7Go quickly and tell his disciples that he has risen from the dead;
and behold, he is going ahead of you into Galilee, there you will see him; behold, I have told
you.

What was the most gentle and yet believable way that the disciples could
receive the message that this Jesus who they knew, who they saw crucified,
who they saw dead was again alive? The most gentle and believable way was
by announcement of an empty tomb. Not some passerby announcing the tomb
was empty and not some Roman soldier’s report. This announcement had to
have a higher credibility. So, God chose an angel! There is no more powerful
messenger than an angel.
The angel said:
1. Do not be afraid. This was similar to the angelic announcement of Jesus’
birth.
2. I know why you are here – you are seeking Jesus who was crucified.
3. He is not here.
4. He is risen – AS HE SAID. It was important to establish the fact that Jesus
was a true prophet. This very fact established it, because he said this was
going to happen.
5. Come, look and see for yourselves – do not take my word for it; he is not
there anymore.
6. Go tell the others!
While the actual message was a simple statement of fact, the delivery of the
message was a dramatic event. The drama got their undivided attention while
the message simply showed them that the door of clarity was in fact open.
When we are faced with tragedy, doubt and grief
are we open to hearing the word of God through whatever messenger
He may choose to assure us that the door of clarity is in fact open?

Matthew 28:8-10: (NASB) 8And they left the tomb quickly with fear and great joy and ran
to report it to his disciples. 9And behold, Jesus met them and greeted them. And they came up
and took hold of his feet and worshiped him. 10Then Jesus said to them, Do not be afraid; go
and take word to my brethren to leave for Galilee, and there they will see me.
For this second step to be a powerful follow-up to the angelic announcement,
Jesus would have to appear as himself. There really was no choice, because
human nature needs a solid base on which to build a life-changing belief. This
second step adds personal recognition to their received information. Had Jesus
appeared as anything other than the old familiar Jesus, it would not have been
believable. It was a logical second step. He did not push them away; he let
them touch and worship him and gave them the ability to have a feel for the
communion they once had with him before.
What message does Jesus personally give them? There are four parts to the
message.
1. He told them not to be afraid.
2. He told them to go tell the others. Make sure they know this. Spread it by
word of mouth.
3. He told them to instruct his brethren to go to Galilee.
4. He told them, “Do not worry; I am not going to disappear; I am going to see
you again in Galilee.”
Jesus not only looked familiar, he acted in a familiar way by giving them
assurance and instruction. This combination added to the angelic
announcement began to address their doubts and enhanced the reality of the
open door of clarity.
Do we find our doubts addressed when we go back to read and meditate
on our risen Lord and his mission? Are we familiar enough with Jesus
to see him and be guided by him to greater clarity?
Angels and recognizing Jesus –
a good start, but we have just scratched the surface!

In this step, Mary Magdalene plays an important role in the faith of the Apostle
John.
An Intimate Moment with Mary Magdalene, Moments with the Savior, Ken Gire
(Only an excerpt from the reading is shown here. Please listen to the audio of our
program or refer to the book.)
•
It was in a garden ages ago that paradise was lost, and it is in a garden now
that it would be regained. But Mary Magdalene doesn’t know that. For her,
the hobnail boot of the Roman Empire has crushed her hope and ground it in
the dirt with its iron heel. Her hope was Jesus. He had changed her life, and
she had followed him ever since. He had cast seven demons out of her,
freeing her from untold torment. He had given her life…a reason to live…a
place in his kingdom…he had given her worth and dignity…understanding…
compassion…love…and he had given her hope. Now that hope lies at the
bottom of her heart, flat and lifeless. But something helps her survive the
cruel boot. Something resilient, like a blade of grass that springs up after
being stepped on. That something is love. Love brought Mary to his cross.
And love brings her now to his grave.
This text is from the Road to Emmaus account as the Apostles explained
their experience to Jesus:
Luke 24:22-24: (NASB) 22But also some women among us amazed us. When they were at the
tomb early in the morning, 23and did not find his body, they came, saying that they had also
seen a vision of angels who said that he was alive. 24Some of those who were with us went to
the tomb and found it just exactly as the women also had said; but him they did not see.
An Intimate Moment with Mary Magdalene, Moments with the Savior, Ken Gire
(Please listen to the audio of our program or refer to the book.)
We know what happened – the women told as they were supposed to tell (this
is faith in action). The disciples were not quite convinced, so they had to run
and see for themselves (this is faith being tested). You cannot blame them. It
is a normal response. We do that all the time if somebody tells us something,
we say, no we must go look for ourselves. It is not a bad thing, especially
under the tragic and doubtful clouds they had lived under for the last few days.
So, they ran and they found an empty tomb. The only thing they were
convinced of was that Jesus was not there, except for John, whose faith was at
this moment stronger. He believed.

A scriptural account of our readings from “Moments with the Savior”:
John 20:2-10: (NASB) 2So she (Mary Magdalene) ran and came to Simon Peter and to the
other disciple whom Jesus loved (John), and said to them, They have taken away the Lord out
of the tomb, and we do not know where they have laid him. 3So Peter and the other disciple
went forth, and they were going to the tomb. (They needed to see for themselves.) 4The two
were running together; and the other disciple ran ahead faster than Peter and came to the tomb
first; 5and stooping and looking in, he saw the linen wrappings lying there; but (out of respect
for Peter, the other disciple waited to enter the tomb) he did not go in. 6And so Simon Peter
also came, following him, and entered the tomb; and he saw the linen wrappings lying there,
7and the face-cloth which had been on his head, not lying with the linen wrappings, but rolled

up in a place by itself. 8So the other disciple who had first come to the tomb then also entered,
and he saw and believed.
Obviously, this was an important step – the women already believed because
they saw him, but John believed simply because the grave was empty. Why did
Peter not believe? Perhaps because of his denials of Jesus he had a longer road
to firmness of faith than John.
9For as yet they did not understand the Scripture, that he must rise again from the dead. 10So
the disciples went away again to their own homes.
What we are observing is a slow, methodical process of conviction: an angelic
announcement, an interchange with a familiar Jesus and the message of these
things relayed to others. Now the others must find their own footing. Faith
cannot always have dramatic events unfolding for it to be built. Sometimes
we are called upon to believe based upon the most basic facts – the tomb is
empty, he is therefore risen.
Do we intentionally face our doubts with a willingness
to build our faith based on the basics? Are we willing to accept
God’s will is present, even if we do not understand it?
Something startling and new happens:

John 20:11-16: (NASB) 11But Mary was standing outside the tomb weeping; and so, as she
wept, she stooped and looked into the tomb; 12and she saw two angels in white sitting, one at
the head and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had been lying. 13And they said to her,
Woman, why are you weeping? She said to them, Because they have taken away my Lord, and I
do not know where they have laid him. 14When she had said this, she turned around and saw
Jesus standing there, and did not know that it was Jesus. 15Jesus said to her, Woman, why are
you weeping? Whom are you seeking? Supposing him to be the gardener, she said to him, Sir, if
you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away. 16Jesus
said to her, Mary! She turned and said to him in Hebrew, Rabboni! (which means, Teacher).

Here is Jesus’ first appearance in an unrecognizable form. He chose to appear
this way before a woman, which is very significant. Even though Mary had not
yet comprehended his resurrection, she seemed to be searching for answers as
she could not seem to stay away from the tomb. She was evidently the most
ready to receive Jesus in whatever form he would reveal himself.
An Intimate Moment with Mary Magdalene, Moments With the Savior, Ken Gire

Please note the explanation below regarding the small apparent contradiction
in the reading quotation that asserts Mary Magdalene as the first person to see
Jesus. This is quoted from Mark 16:9 and contradicts Matthew 28:1-10.
(Source: Biblical commentary by C.T. Russell) Omitted in the Sinaitic and Vatican manuscripts.
Evidently Mark’s Gospel was originally incomplete and someone undertook to finish it about the
fifth century. The fifth century Alexandrian manuscript is the oldest to contain the last 12
verses. These verses are spurious according to the American Standard Version, the Diaglott and
the Revised Version.
John 20:17-18: (NASB) 17Jesus said to her, Stop clinging to me, for I have not yet ascended
to the Father; but go to my brethren and say to them, I ascend to my Father and your Father,
and my God and your God. 18Mary Magdalene came, announcing to the disciples, I have seen the
Lord, and that he had said these things to her.
Jesus needed to establish the fact that his nature had changed, that he was the
same in character yet entirely different in nature, because flesh and blood had
been replaced by a spiritual being. This was radical and was his first revealing
on such a level. Mary recognized his voice and not the way he looked.
Jesus’ message to Mary:
1. I am going to stay awhile as I have more convincing to do.
2. But he stressed the fact: I am going to ascend.
You have two elements here that demonstrate a change of nature:
1. He does not look the same.
2. He has the ability to ascend. In one occurrence, here he has given two
evidences that he is not the same flesh and blood Jesus that they knew.
From angelic announcement, to appearing in a recognizable and familiar
fashion, to faith without seeing, to appearing in an unrecognizable state, Jesus
was methodically and gently revealing the magnitude of the effects of his
resurrection. Small steps give opportunity to find clarity as one seeks
understanding.
Are we carefully observing the small steps of clarity Jesus gives
us as we wrestle with our personal tragedies and doubts?

How do you help many to believe in something
they have NEVER seen before?

Hope being given clarity:
25And he said to them, O foolish men and slow of heart to believe in all that the prophets have
spoken! 26Was it not necessary for the Christ to suffer these things and to enter into his glory?
27Then beginning with Moses and with all the prophets, he explained to them the things
concerning himself in all the Scriptures. 28And they approached the village where they were
going, and he acted as though he were going farther. 29But they urged him, saying, Stay with
us, for it is getting toward evening, and the day is now nearly over. So, he went in to stay with
them. 30When he had reclined at the table with them, he took the bread and blessed it, and

breaking it, he began giving it to them. 31Then their eyes were opened and they recognized him;
and he vanished from their sight. 32They said to one another, Were not our hearts burning within
us while he was speaking to us on the road, while he was explaining the Scriptures to us?
An Intense Moment on the Emmaus Road, Moments with the Savior, Ken Gire
(Please listen to the audio of our program or refer to the book.)
Jesus again proved (this time to two disciples) that he was no longer a man and
that what he looked like to them did not define who he was. He became
recognizable by what he did, showing that he was still their loving and devoted
master. Further, he was able to vanish from their sight. Step by step, element
by element, they are beginning to understand the magnitude of who and what
their Lord is.
Do we allow the magnitude of who and what Jesus is to
overwhelm us with clarity in the face of our tragedies and doubts?
Up to this point Jesus appeared to one, two or three. Now that he had
begun expanding the minds of a few and given them the ability to
communicate their experiences, he again appears miraculously to several:
Luke 24:33-37: (NASB) 33And they got up that very hour and returned to Jerusalem, and
found gathered together the eleven and those who were with them, 34saying, The Lord has really
risen and has appeared to Simon. 35They began to relate their experiences on the road and how
he was recognized by them in the breaking of the bread. 36While they were telling these things,
he himself stood in their midst and said to them, Peace be to you. 37But they were startled and
frightened and thought that they were seeing a spirit.
This startled reaction was in part because they were in a locked room.
John 20:19: (NASB) So when it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and
when the doors were shut where the disciples were, for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and
stood in their midst and said to them, Peace be with you.

Not only was Jesus capable of vanishing, he could also pass through walls or
doors!
Luke 24:38-49: (NASB) 38And he said to them, Why are you troubled, and why do doubts
arise in your hearts? 39See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself; touch me and see, for a
spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have. 40And when he had said this, he
showed them his hands and his feet. 41While they still could not believe it because of their joy
and amazement, he said to them, Have you anything here to eat? 42They gave him a piece of a
broiled fish; 43and he took it and ate it before them.
Jesus obviously appeared in his recognizable form and furthered their ability to
comprehend him by showing them things they could identify with. He showed
them his hands, feet (perhaps the wounds of the cross) and that he could eat
with them.
44Now he said to them, These are my words which I spoke to you while I was still with you, that
all things which are written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must
be fulfilled. 45Then he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures, 46and he said to them,
Thus it is written, that the Christ would suffer and rise again from the dead the third day…
Jesus then tied his own words together with the words of prophecy as the
absolute proof of what had happened, and how it was that he was now
miraculously standing before them.
47and that repentance for forgiveness of sins would be proclaimed in his name to all the nations,
beginning from Jerusalem. 48You are witnesses of these things. 49And behold, I am sending forth
the promise of my Father upon you; but you are to stay in the city until you are clothed with
power from on high.
And now Jesus for the first time adds into his explanation their part – their
responsibility going forward to him and to the Gospel.
The journey of clarity for Jesus’ followers continues as Jesus appears as
himself, though now he shows several followers that he can pass through
inanimate objects at will. He is the same Jesus, yet so very different as he
now as a spirit being and no longer human, obviously wielded a spiritual power
they could not even comprehend.
Are we cognizant of the ever-present and ever-powerful existence
of Jesus in all aspects of our lives? Does his presence bring us
clarity and peace as we face our personal doubts?

With all this proof of the risen Jesus,
was there still room for doubt? Yes, there was!
With all the varied appearances of Jesus in such a short time, the Apostles and
disciples had much to work with. They had angelic announcement, they had
Jesus appear multiple times in a familiar form as well as in an unfamiliar form,
and he could come and go miraculously. More than all of this, they had Jesus
on several occasions point them to the prophecies of old as infallible proof of
what had happened. He verified those prophecies by reminding them of his
own words! Yes, he had indeed been raised – raised to a glory beyond their
wildest imaginations!
With all of this we can still doubt. Thomas was in that little boat of doubt. He
had not yet himself seen the risen Lord and was called upon to trust in the
accounts of the others.
Thomas was not there in the last revealing step behind locked doors, as we
see from the continuation of the John text:
John 20:24-29: (NASB) 24But Thomas, one of the twelve, called Didymus, was not with them
when Jesus came. 25So the other disciples were saying to him, We have seen the Lord! But he
said to them, Unless I see in his hands the imprint of the nails, and put my finger into the place
of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.
I will not believe – unless - such are the proclamations of those of us who might
be in that little boat of doubt with Thomas. Such a boat has no anchor of trust
and finds itself listing about as we think and wish, as we wonder and second
guess and as we are reduced to desperately clinging to the sides of that little
boat, ever fearful of capsizing. Jesus understands doubt, and if we are willing,
he will gently show us how to step out of that little boat of doubt and into the
unsinkable vessel of his love and power.
26After eight days his disciples were again inside, and Thomas with them. Jesus came, the doors
having been shut, and stood in their midst and said, Peace be with you. 27Then he said to Thomas,
Reach here with your finger, and see my hands; and reach here your hand and put it into my
side; and do not be unbelieving, but believing. 28Thomas answered and said to him, my Lord and
my God! 29Jesus said to him, Because you have seen me, have you believed? Blessed are they
who did not see, and yet believed.

Jesus faces the doubts of Thomas with the truth. He not only shows Thomas
exactly what he needs to see, he demonstrates his spiritual power by
recounting what Thomas had said eight days ago! Jesus had already invisibly
been in the presence of Thomas, it is just that Thomas could not see him!
Thomas immediately displays the humility and faith that had been left behind
when he boarded that little boat of doubt. Thomas leaps from his little boat of
doubt as he worships the risen Lord!
Sometimes because of tragedy and doubt the clear evidence of truth and hope
that is presented can be ignored. Thomas had his heart in the right place and
Jesus knew just how to reveal himself in such a way that Thomas would again
stand in faith.
Are we too comfortable in our little boat of doubt?
Are we looking for the clarity of Jesus’ presence in our lives,
even when we cannot see him? Even when we cannot see him, he IS there!
We have seen Jesus reveal himself by way of prophecy, miracles, physical
gestures and voice. Now he would reveal himself to his disciples in an even
more familiar way. He would help them, feed them and teach them as he had
done so often before. He would now also remove the clouds of guilt that they
had stubbornly covered themselves with.
John 21:1-3: (NASB) 1After these things Jesus manifested himself again to the disciples at
the Sea of Tiberias, and he manifested himself in this way. 2Simon Peter, and Thomas… and

A Final Intimate Moment With Peter, Moments with the Savior, Ken Gire
(Only an excerpt from the reading is shown here. Please listen to the audio of our
program or refer to the book.)
•
What do you do when you’ve failed a friend? After you’ve cried till you’re numb.
After you’ve replayed the failure over and over in your mind. After you’ve run

yourself down and can’t think of any more names to call yourself. What do you
do then? You find some way to hold back the pain. “I’m going fishing.” That
is Peter’s way of dealing with the pain. He’s tired of thinking. He’s tired of
the incriminating conversations he’s had with himself.
He wants a mindless
diversion, an escape. But the sea is unsympathetic. And the night refuses him
a reprieve. In the melancholy darkness, Peter is lulled by the rhythmic slapping
of waves against the boat. His mind ebbs nostalgically back…back…back to when
Jesus was in the boat with them and calmed the storm…back to when he walked
on the water…back to when…Thus he passes the night away, throwing out his
net and catching only slippery moments from the past. Memories. That’s all
he’s got now. But one of those memories he wishes he could throw back: how
he stood there when Jesus needed him the most…stood there and denied even
knowing him…cursed and swore and, and…

fish, do you? They answered him, No. 6And he said to them, Cast the net on the right-hand side

because of the great number of fish.

and although there were so many, the net was not torn. 12Jesus said to them, Come and have
breakfast. (It sounds like Jesus never left.) None of the disciples ventured to question him, Who
are you? knowing that it was the Lord. 13Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them,
and the fish likewise.
A Final Intimate Moment With Peter, Moments with the Savior, Ken Gire
(Please listen to the audio of our program or refer to the book.)
This was a powerful moment as these humble fishermen are face to face with
Jesus and FINALLY, no one had to ask, “Who are you?” They all KNEW. With
their knowledge came a sense of awe and an even deeper sense of humility as
well as an awareness of the clouds of guilt that haunted them.
A Final Intimate Moment With Peter, Moments with the Savior, Ken Gire
(Please listen to the audio of our program or refer to the book.)
Jesus’ tender forgiveness towards a guilt-ridden Peter took this step of
revealing himself to a whole new level because it gave his followers a
profoundly practical sense of clarity. This Jesus was undoubtedly the same in
character but he also carried a depth of godliness that transcended human
capacity. Peter especially would change as a result of this new beginning.
A Final Intimate Moment With Peter, Moments with the Savior, Ken Gire
(Please listen to the audio of our program or refer to the book.)

The risen Jesus in these last two revealing steps addressed and dissolved two of
the most debilitating experiences of the human condition – doubt with Thomas
and guilt with Peter. The clarity and familiarity of his message to both
troubled men changed them.
Are we willing to have Jesus change us? Do we tenaciously cling to our little
boat of doubt and stubbornly persist under our dark cloud of guilt or are we
willing to face our Lord, see his works, hear his words and accept his love?
What more could we possibly hope for from the risen Jesus?

There was world changing work to be done as a result of his change!
